introduction: On this Sunday, Sirach says that a person's words reveal what is in their heart, as fruit reveals the tree. In the Gospel, Jesus warns us to take the log out of our own eye before removing the splinter from our brother's eye, and says that a good tree bears good fruit. Paul proclaims that death is swallowed up in victory. Let us ask the Lord to make our hearts good.

prayerOfTheFaithful.invitation: Brothers and sisters, it is good to give thanks to the Lord. Let us bring him our prayers.
intentions: For the Church: that her words and actions may bear the good fruit of the Gospel. Let us pray to the Lord.
For teachers, leaders and all who guide others: that they may first let Christ guide them. Let us pray to the Lord.
For those who are quick to judge and slow to forgive: that God may give them humble hearts. Let us pray to the Lord.
For those who are afraid of death: that they may trust in Christ's victory. Let us pray to the Lord.
For ourselves: that the words of our mouths may come from hearts full of goodness. Let us pray to the Lord.
prayerOfTheFaithful.conclusion: Lord God, you know what is in our hearts. Make them good and fruitful, so that our words and works may give you glory. Through Christ our Lord.

reflection.title: The log in your own eye
reflection.body:
The Book of Sirach uses simple images from daily life. When grain is sifted, the husks are left behind; when a potter fires a pot, the kiln shows whether it is sound. In the same way, "The fruit of a tree discloses its cultivation, so is the utterance of the thought of a person's heart." Our words show who we are.

Jesus takes up the same theme. He begins with a question: "Can the blind guide the blind? Won't they both fall into a pit?" Then he gives a picture that is almost comic: someone with a large beam in his own eye trying to remove a speck from his brother's eye. "You hypocrite! First remove the beam from your own eye, and then you can see clearly to remove the speck of chaff that is in your brother's eye." We are often quick to see the faults of others and slow to see our own.

Jesus is not saying we can never correct anyone. He is saying we must begin with ourselves. Only someone who has humbly faced their own sin can help another with gentleness.

Then he speaks of trees and fruit: "For each tree is known by its own fruit." And he goes to the root: "The good man out of the good treasure of his heart brings out that which is good... for out of the abundance of the heart, his mouth speaks." If we want our words to be good, our hearts must be changed.

Paul ends his great chapter on the resurrection with a shout of victory: "Death is swallowed up in victory." And he concludes, "be steadfast, immovable, always abounding in the Lord's work, because you know that your labor is not in vain."

This week, before criticizing anyone, stop and ask: what is the beam in my own eye? Listen to your own words, and ask God to heal the heart they come from.
